title: Gathin23/cleanyourtv
author: Gathin23
body:
**The viral tweet:** [x.com/gathint/status/2111379569030939102](https://x.com/gathint/status/2111379569030939102) On 17 October 2026 I posted a before and after of my parents' TV, cleaned up by Claude Code over Wi-Fi. It reached 7.4M views, people started doing the same to their own TVs, and their replies turned into the lists here: 170+ TV models from 200+ contributors in four days. The repo was called tv-vibehack until the 19th; old links work. **Themes, switches and add-ons:** [cleanyour.tv/addons](https://cleanyour.tv/addons) **Official links:** the website is [cleanyour.tv](https://cleanyour.tv) and the code, launcher and tools live only in this repo. Other domains using the name, such as cleanyourtv.com, are not run by this project ([#1004](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/issues/1004)). ## How it works Android TVs have the same debug bridge as Android phones. Switch on USB debugging in the TV's developer options, allow your computer once, and the rest is standard Android tooling: | Step | What happens | |---|---| | **Back up** | The list of installed packages and settings. | | **Disable** | The manufacturer's telemetry, ad services, content rows and preloaded junk, with `pm disable-user`. Nothing is uninstalled, so a restore script can undo every step. | | **Install** | A small native launcher, made the default home screen. | **No root, no cable, nothing uninstalled, and a one-line restore if you change your mind.** The bloat differs by brand, so the prompt has your coding assistant discover it on your TV and ask before touching anything you might use. ## Quick start | You have | Do this | |---|---| | **A computer** | Use the prompt with a coding assistant: the three steps below. | | **Only an Android phone** | Use the community-built [Clean Your TV app](https://cleanyour.tv/app) by [@udhaykumarbala](https://github.com/udhaykumarbala): connect, analyse, clean, in about five minutes. No laptop, no coding agent. | With a computer, you need it on the same Wi-Fi as the TV and a coding assistant with shell access. Any of these work: Claude Code (on [0G Private Computer](https://pc.0g.ai) or an [Anthropic plan](https://claude.com/pricing)), [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) or [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli). | Where | What to do | |---|---| | **1. On the TV** | Settings → Device Preferences → About → press OK on **Build** seven times → back → Developer options → **USB debugging** on. If you see a Network or ADB debugging toggle, turn that on too. Keep the TV on. | | **2. On your computer** | Paste [`PROMPT.md`](PROMPT.md) into your assistant and fill in your TV model. | | **3. Follow along** | Accept "Allow USB debugging?" on the TV, then answer the checklist: which apps you use, the dock size and app order, whether to keep the voice assistant, Chromecast and updates. | The assistant backs up, debloats, builds and installs the launcher, and checks each step with screenshots pulled from the TV. With this repo as context it takes about fifteen minutes. ## What you get A home screen that looks like an Apple TV and gets out of the way: | Part | What it looks like | |---|---| | **A pitch-black home** | A dock of your four favourite apps in a rounded band, where Apple TV puts it. | | **A top shelf** | Names the focused app in large type, with an ambient glow in a colour taken from its artwork. | | **The rest of your apps in a grid** | Slides up when you press Down. | | **One floating glass highlight** | Springs from tile to tile. The focused tile lifts and shows its name. | | **Three frosted buttons** | Inputs (HDMI ports under the names you gave them in the TV's settings, AV, Live TV), Wi-Fi or Ethernet with the network name, Settings. | | **A greeting, a thin clock and the date** | In [Outfit](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Outfit), and a matching Clock screensaver. Set `show_stats` in config or a theme for one line under the clock: CPU, free memory and free storage. It stays off unless you turn it on, and it refreshes only while Home is on screen. | | **Themes and module cards** | Themes change colours, wallpaper, dock and columns without a rebuild, and module cards let other apps plug a tile in, only with your say-so. | And a TV that stops working against you: no sponsored rows, no "Discover" nags, no analytics phoning home, no apps you never asked for. | | | |---|---| | ![The top shelf names the focused app over an ambient glow in its colour](docs/focus-2-up-netflix.png) | ![The Inputs popup: HDMI ports with what is connected, AV and Live TV](docs/inputs-menu.jpg) | | *Top shelf and ambient glow* | *Inputs: HDMI with connection state, AV, Live TV* | | ![The grid with the glass highlight on a tile and its name beneath](docs/focus-1-fancode.png) | ![The Clock screensaver: a thin clock drifting over the glow](docs/clock-screensaver.png) | | *The grid, one glass highlight, the tile's name* | *Clock screensaver, drifts so nothing burns in* | | ![The aurora theme: a wallpaper and tinted pills, pushed without a rebuild](themes/aurora/screenshot.jpg) | ![Six columns and a six-app dock from a theme's config.json](themes/six-columns/screenshot.jpg) | | *Aurora theme, pushed with `tools/theme.sh`* | *Six columns and a six-app dock, same launcher* | | ![Moving a tile: held OK, chose Move, the tile is picked up and the others dim](docs/tile-move.jpg) | ![The App library: installed apps, one press adds an app back to Home](docs/app-library.jpg) | | *With `tile_menu`, hold OK on a tile, Move: arrows carry it, Back puts it down* | *App library: one press puts a removed app back on Home* | ## Supported TVs Anything running **Android TV** or **Google TV**. | Platform | What works | |---|---| | **Android TV, Google TV** | The debloat and the launcher. | | **Fire TV** | The debloat half only, since Fire OS will not hand Home to a third-party launcher. And on the 2015 Fire TV Box (Fire OS 5) even that half fails: every `pm` route is refused. | | **A few China-market TCL sets** | They refuse to install any launcher at all; their lists say so in the header. | | **Samsung (Tizen), LG (webOS)** | Different systems. See [SHOWCASE.md](SHOWCASE.md#other-platforms-fire-tv-and-lg-webos) for three webOS ports, and [docs/devices/samsung-tizen.md](docs/devices/samsung-tizen.md) for what a 2021 Samsung set answers over Wi-Fi (no ADB, so no `pm disable-user`) if you are weighing a Tizen port. | Tested lists from contributors, one folder per model in [`examples/`](examples/): **TCL** 64 · **Sony** 37 · **Xiaomi** 31 · **Philips** 15 · **Hisense** 10 · **Skyworth** 9 · **Amazon Fire TV** 7 · **BenQ** 4 · **OnePlus** 4 · **Panasonic** 4 · **Thomson** 4 · **Google** 3 · **Haier** 3 · **JVC** 3 · **SHARP** 3 · **Vu** 3 · **CHiQ** 2 · **FFalcon** 2 · **Hitachi** 2 · **Kalley** 2 · **Kogan** 2 · **Motorola** 2 · **Nokia** 2 · **NVIDIA Shield** 2 · **onn** 2 · **RCA** 2 · **Redmi** 2 · **RockTek** 2 · **Sankey** 2 · **Toshiba** 2 · **Vidda** 2 · Acer · AiPro2K · AIWA · AQUA · Artel · ASUS · Beko · Caxium · Cecotec · Challenger · Compac · Dcolor · Dialog · EKO · Freebox · Grundig · INCLO · Insignia Fire TV · Karbonn · KTC · Liberton · Lumio · Master-G · MTC · Noblex · OK. · Panavox · PEAQ · Polytron · PRISM+ · SANYO · Sber · Super General · Tele System · TiVo · Tornado · Turkcell · Tuvio · Verizon · Vision · Anker Nebula, BYINTEK, Epson, Formovie, Gadnic, HOTACK, JMGO, Magcubic, Portronics, Stellamore, Wanbo and XGIMI projectors

Windows (PowerShell) Every script has a PowerShell twin next to it. On Windows with Android Studio installed nothing else is needed: ```powershell python -m venv tools\venv; tools\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r tools\requirements.txt powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File launcher\build-and-install.ps1 -TvHost 192.168.1.50 powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\disable.ps1 -TvHost 192.168.1.50 examples\xiaomi-mi-tv-4a\debloat.txt ```
How the scripts protect Home The install scripts ask the TV which launcher owns Home and only disable one they recognise, the four in `KNOWN_STOCK_LAUNCHERS`: `com.google.android.tvlauncher`, `com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx`, `com.google.android.leanbacklauncher` and Xiaomi's `com.mitv.tvhome` (PatchWall). Pass `STOCK_LAUNCHER=` (`-StockLauncher`) to override, or `none` to leave it alone. `tools/disable.sh` (`disable.ps1`) applies the same rule before it disables anything: if the list contains the app that owns Home and no other app on the TV answers HOME, it skips that entry, says why, and disables the rest of the list. The setup wizard, the settings apps, a vendor `FallbackHome` and factory-test apps (Xiaomi's `com.duokan.factorytest`) answer HOME too and don't count. So a list applied before the launcher handover cannot leave the TV with nothing to start. Run the same list again once `launcher/build-and-install.sh` has made the new launcher Home and the entry is applied; `FORCE_HOME=1` (`$env:FORCE_HOME`) disables it anyway.
Where your lists can live Debloat list paths passed to `disable.sh` and `restore.sh` are relative to the directory you run from, so your own lists can live outside the repository. Absolute paths also work.
## The microphone, and what can be said about it "Which of these packages is listening?" has no honest one-line answer, and a permission scan makes it worse: on many sets most packages run as `android.uid.system`, so fifty of them show `RECORD_AUDIO: granted=true` and none of them record anything. On others the microphone is in the remote, not the panel, and a package with no audio permission at all still sees everything on screen — ACR clients such as `tv.inscape.tvclient.inscapeacr` identify content from the picture and need only `INTERNET`. `tools/privacy.py` reports what the TV actually says instead of guessing: `TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/privacy.py` prints voice, ACR and telemetry candidates in three groups, each with its evidence — named by the firmware's own `voice_interaction_service`, a known component from [`examples/`](examples/), or nothing but a matching name — plus whether the package declares `RECORD_AUDIO`, whether it shares the system UID, and whether the returned AppOps history contains microphone access. A configured mode or a rejected attempt alone is not evidence of access. `--write privacy.txt` turns the identified candidates into a normal debloat list, so applying it and undoing it are the commands you already use (`tools/disable.sh`, `tools/restore.sh`). Packages that only matched by name stay out unless you pass `--include-low`; they are the ones to check with `dumpsys package ` first. What the audit cannot do is prove intent. `appops` shows an op was touched, not what happened to the stream afterwards, and no scan of package names proves a TV is or is not recording. Disabling an assistant is a trade you make with a specific loss (the remote's mic button, voice search inside apps), which is why the report names that loss per package instead of calling it a win. ## The launcher A small native home screen for Android TV: **about 517 KB**, plain Java, built for TVs with 1 GB of RAM. No blur, no video, no network permission, no background services. The **TV** needs Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer: `minSdk` is a compile-time floor in [`launcher/app/build.gradle`](launcher/app/build.gradle), and the install script asks the TV for `ro.build.version.sdk` before it builds, so an older set is told both numbers instead of failing at `pm install` (see [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md) for what is left on such a set). | What | How it works | |---|---| | **Configure** | Dock order, hidden apps, Live TV app, 4 to 7 tiles per row, reduced motion. Build it yourself It needs JDK 17 and Android SDK platform 34. On macOS: `brew install openjdk@17 android-commandlinetools` and `sdkmanager "platforms;android-34" "build-tools;34.0.0"`. On Linux the install script finds `~/Android/Sdk` and the `java` on your PATH.
Configure [`config.xml`](launcher/app/src/main/res/values/config.xml) sets the dock order, hidden apps, the Live TV package, columns (tiles shrink from 5 up), rows under the dock, an optional VPN app for the network pill, and `reduced_motion` for TVs whose GPU cannot keep up. Themes set the same keys plus a background colour and a wallpaper.
Launcher settings and the default home - Click **Settings** for the TV's own settings. Hold OK on it for its menu: **Launcher settings** (with `launcher_settings_button` a click opens those instead and the menu leaves the row out), **Native settings** where the TV ships a settings app of its own beside Android's - Xiaomi China, TCL/FFALCON and Fire OS are in `settings_fallback_components` - because that app holds pages Android's has no row for, such as Xiaomi's Account & Security with the ADB switch; **Module cards** with `module_cards`; **Edit dock** with `dock_row`; and **Reorder apps**. The launcher's own page has these rows, top to bottom: - **Reorder apps**, only with `launcher_settings_button`: OK picks an app up, the arrows move it, Back places it, and Back again finishes. - **Apps per row** 4, 5, 6 or 7; **Rows below dock** 0 to 3, how many rows of tiles stay visible under the dock band; **Dock band opacity** 100%, 70%, 50% or 30%. The last two only do anything while the dock is its own row (`dock_row`, on by default). - **Wallpaper**: one picture from the theme's collection (or its `wallpaper.jpg`), **None**, or **Theme default**. A pick holds that picture and stops the rotation until you choose Theme default, press Follow theme, or push the theme again. - **Animations** on or off, and **Advanced effects** (tile lift, icon zoom and smooth ambient-colour transitions; they may use more memory) once animations are on. - **Open on start**, only with `open_on_start_choice`: Off, or an app that opens instead of Home the first time Home comes up after the TV starts. Once per boot, so Home and Back still reach the launcher. - **Follow theme (reset on-TV choices)**, which clears every choice above. Pushing or resetting a theme clears them too. - **Choose default home** opens Android's home picker, and **TV system settings** the TV's own settings page. - **Change the default home:** Launcher settings and the optional Default-home tile (`show_home_settings_shortcut`) open Android's home picker. Choose the original launcher to stop using CleanYourTV as Home, or CleanYourTV to return. The original launcher must be enabled; if the install script disabled it, run the restore script below first. Some TVs provide no home picker.
Languages English, German, Danish, Spanish, Catalan, French, Russian, Serbian (Latin), Polish, Czech, Italian, Portuguese, Turkish, Arabic, Hebrew, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese (Taiwan), Thai, Finnish, Vietnamese, Bangla, Indonesian, Norwegian Bokmål, Dutch, Uzbek (Latin), Ukrainian and Korean. The launcher follows the TV's language. Android 13+ can set it for the launcher alone: `tools/tv.py 'cmd locale set-app-locales com.gathin.tvhome --locales ca'`. Hebrew mirrors the layout: menu buttons on the left, date and clock on the right with the greeting above, dock and app rows starting on the right with matching remote navigation, the input selector's icons and labels on the right, and dates with the month prefix ב (for example, 19 באוקטובר). The Clock screensaver right-aligns its date and time. Russian covers every screen, including race weekends, festival greetings and the Shamsi date. Other languages keep their original layouts.
Module cards Any TV app can declare its own tile (label, caption, glow). The launcher asks you once per app, keeps it hidden by default, and remembers the answer for that app's signing key and card name. Hold OK on Settings and choose Module cards to change your mind. How to make one: [`docs/modules.md`](docs/modules.md); the contract: [`docs/specs/card.md`](docs/specs/card.md).
Clock screensaver Pick "Clock" in the TV's screensaver settings, or over ADB: ```bash tools/tv.py 'settings put secure screensaver_components com.gathin.tvhome/.ClockDream; settings put secure screensaver_enabled 1' ```
Remote keys - An optional accessibility service keeps the remote's **Input** button working on Google TV (`INPUT_KEY_SERVICE=1` at install). - It can bring back other buttons only the stock launcher answered, such as the **YouTube** button (`app_keys` and `input_key_keycodes`, in config.xml or a theme; `HOME_KEY_SERVICE=1` reads `app_keys` too). - A `hold:` prefix on an `app_keys` entry gives that button a second app: a normal press opens the unprefixed app, holding for half a second opens the hold one (by keycode or `hold:scan:...`). - In place of an app, an `app_keys` entry can name an action: `back`, `home`, `recents`, `mute`, `sleep`, `screensaver`, `settings` or `wifi`, so a spare colour button can mute the TV or, held, put it in standby. - `HOME_KEY_SERVICE=1` also fixes sticks whose Home key sends ALL_APPS, and opens Settings from the remote's **gear** button, even one Android does not map (scancodes or keycodes in config.xml). - With `settings_key_panel` the gear opens a [small quick settings panel](docs/quick-settings-panel.jpg) over Home or any app: TV settings, Display, Network, Apps and Launcher settings.
Navigation and artwork Up and Down move one row. The top buttons never fall through to tiles, and Down from them returns to the dock tile you came from. The last focused app is remembered, and installing or removing an app refreshes the tiles while Home is open. App banners load at xhdpi or better, so low-density TV UIs do not downsample them before the focus zoom.
## Restoring your TV Keep the list you applied. One line puts the TV back the way it was: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/restore.sh examples//debloat.txt # Android TV TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/restore.sh examples//debloat.txt com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx # Google TV ``` | What | How | |---|---| | **A record comes first** | Before `tools/disable.sh` changes anything it writes down what the TV looked like, in `~/.cleanyourtv/`. | | **Restore replays it** | A package you had disabled yourself stays disabled, and Home goes back to the component that owned it. | | **The launcher stays installed** | Remove it from the TV's Settings → Apps if you want it gone. | | **No computer?** | If the TV is unreachable, its own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages too. |
What the record holds, and what happens without one Before `tools/disable.sh` changes anything it writes down what the TV looked like: for every package in the list whether it was enabled, already disabled or not installed, which component owned Home, and the three animation scales. That record lives in `~/.cleanyourtv/`, one file per TV and list, and a second run of the same list keeps the first record instead of saving the cleaned-up state over it. If you added packages to the list since, that run adds them to the record before disabling them. Keep the list you applied. The restore script replays the record, so a package you had disabled yourself stays disabled and Home goes back to the component that owned it: The `stock launcher` argument is only a fallback: with a record, the launcher that actually owned Home is the one that gets it back, and the argument is used only when nothing answered HOME at the time or this project's launcher owned it. The stock launcher is enabled again either way, unless it was already disabled when the record was taken. Without a record (an older run, or a record you deleted) the script says so and falls back to enabling the whole list and resetting the scales to `1.0`, which is what it used to do. It leaves the new launcher installed (remove it from the TV's Settings → Apps if you want it gone) and does not know about packages you disabled outside the list. To switch back later, run the install script again; it works out which launcher to disable even when Home has fallen back to Android's chooser. If the TV is unreachable, its own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages too.
## After a firmware update An update installs over the cleaned-up system: the listed packages come back, Home goes to the stock launcher, and new preloads appear that no list mentions. Nothing else here notices, so compare the TV with the list you applied: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples//debloat.txt ``` It prints what drifted and exits 1 when anything did, so a weekly job on a home server or a Pi is enough to hear about it: ```bash 0 9 * * 1 cd ~/cleanyourtv && TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples//debloat.txt ``` `--fix` reapplies the list to what drifted: it switches Home to the launcher the list does not disable (pass a package as the second argument if you run a fork), then disables the listed packages that came back, and reads the TV back to confirm both. It writes no recovery record, because the record already holds the state from before the first run: `tools/restore.sh` still returns the TV to stock afterwards. Home is fixed first; if no launcher is left to take it, `--fix` changes nothing and says so. It runs the same safety checks as `tools/disable.sh` before it disables anything, since an update is the moment they matter again: it leaves setupwraith on while the saved Wi-Fi network belongs to it (`FORCE_SETUPWRAITH=1` on Ethernet), leaves the packages under the HDMI/AV inputs on (`TVINPUT_ALLOW=1` if you really want them off), leaves on the apps the TV opens its inputs and Settings with (`HANDLERS_ALLOW=1`), and never takes Home to a vendor `FallbackHome` or a factory-test app. Each package it leaves on comes with the reason and exits 1, because the TV is not back to the list until you deal with that one by hand. With `stock_home_redirect` the stock launcher can stay Home on purpose: the list leaves it out, the install script ran with `STOCK_LAUNCHER=none`, Android keeps it as Home, and `HomeKeyService` sends its home screen on to this launcher. On the Chromecast with Google TV 4K that setup matches the folder's `debloat-keep-cast.txt`, not its `debloat.txt`, which disables setupwraith and the screensaver pair the redirect setup keeps. On the Acer AR55AR2851UDPRO it is the folder's `debloat.txt`. Check those lists with the stock launcher as the second argument. Without it the check expects `com.gathin.tvhome` on Home, so every run reports Home as drift, and `--fix` tries to move Home to it, which those TVs do not keep: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples/google-chromecast-gtv-4k/debloat-keep-cast.txt com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples/acer-ar55ar2851udpro/debloat.txt com.google.android.tvlauncher ``` Leave the argument out where the stock launcher is meant to be off, disabled by the list or by the install script: the Chromecast's `debloat.txt`, where the install script disables launcherx, and the XGIMI projectors, where the redirect only covers for firmware that turns it back on. There the stock launcher on Home is drift, and naming it as the second argument would hide that drift. Lists that also disable the updater get no updates at all. To install one, re-enable the updater on the TV, let it update, run `check.py --fix`, and disable the updater again. On Windows the same command is `tools\venv\Scripts\python.exe -I tools\check.py `. ## When something goes wrong The full list of things that bit us is in [docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md). The three that matter most: - 🍎 **macOS blocks `adb connect`** ("No route to host") under Local Network privacy. `tools/tv.py` avoids the binary. - ⚠️ **Disable the stock launcher only after the new one is installed and running**, or Home lands on a factory test app. The install script orders this for you. - 🔁 **On Google TV the setup wizard** (`com.google.android.tungsten.setupwraith`) can take Home and crash-loop the system after the stock launcher is disabled. Disable it too, and list it in your `debloat.txt` so restore brings it back. But check `dumpsys wifi | grep -o 'cname=[^ ]*'` first: if the Wi-Fi network was saved during setup it belongs to setupwraith, and disabling it deletes the network (re-join it in Settings first; `tools/disable.sh` skips setupwraith until you do). On Google's own Chromecast and on the Google TV Streamer it also costs phone casting, see [Troubleshooting](doc

title: Zagitta/gpu-unlock
author: Zagitta
body:
# GPU unlock 1.0.0

Unlock FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards to their professional equivalents

This Linux kernel module combines the CMP unlocker's V67/PLM technique with the pre-driver timing of the UEFI approach. It runs the unlock, writes the speed selectors (SS0 `0x88888888`, which selects the full BF16 rate, and the 4-bit SS1 `0x8` IMLA4) and performs FLR before the unmodified NVIDIA driver binds the card. It is neither a UEFI application nor a patched NVIDIA driver. 

The benefit of this early kmod driver is that it does not require manual patching each time nvidia releases a new driver version.

The effect of this unlock is that it doubles the instruction issuing speed of FP/BF16 FMA into FP32 operations on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards.

[3090 Ti dense 8192³ GEMM at 450 W, five-sample medians with FP32 accumulation](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/1#issue-5905622687):


| Input | Before       | After         |
| ----- | ------------ | ------------- |
| FP16  | 87.46 TFLOPS | 118.39 TFLOPS |
| BF16  | 87.50 TFLOPS | 157.41 TFLOPS |
| TF32  | 42.58 TFLOPS | 82.61 TFLOPS  |

## Tested cards

Results reported by users. The module accepts every GeForce ID listed in
`kernel/gpu_unlock/main.c`, but the cards below are the ones someone has
reported on. Please add yours with a
[compatibility report](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/new?template=compatibility-report.yml),
whether it worked or not.

| Chip  | Card                              | PCI ID      | Result                              | BF16 GEMM gain | Reports |
| ----- | --------------------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------- | ------- |
| GA102 | RTX 3090 Ti                       | `10de:2203` | Unlocked                            | +68–80%        | [#1](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/1) |
| GA102 | RTX 3090                          | `10de:2204` | Unlocked                            | +25–67%        | [#5](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/5), [#9](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/9), [#10](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/10), [#17](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/17), [#25](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/25), [#27](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/27), [#33](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/33) |
| GA102 | RTX 3080 Ti 20 GB (OEM, GA102-250) | `10de:2205` | Unlock completes, BF16 stays at half rate | —        | [#28](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/28) |
| GA102 | RTX 3080 10 GB                    | `10de:2206` | Unlocked                            | +70–73%        | [#14](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/14) |
| GA102 | RTX 3080 20 GB (memory upgrade)   | `10de:2206` | Unlocked                            | +56–59%        | [#10](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/10), [#15](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/15) |
| GA104 | RTX 3070                          | `10de:2484` | Unlocked                            | +73–81%        | [#10](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/10), [#12](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/12) |
| GA104 | RTX 3070 Ti                       | `10de:2482` | Not tested with this module (the same unlock worked from a UEFI port on Windows) | — | [#32](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/32) |
| GA106 | RTX 3060 12 GB                    | `10de:2504` | Unlocked                            | about +80%     | [#13](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/pull/13), [#31](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/31) |
| GA103 | any                               | `10de:2414` | No reports yet                      | —              | — |

The gains are dense GEMM throughput from each report's own benchmark, so
they are not directly comparable. The power limit matters a lot: the lowest
figure (+25%) is from cards capped at 225 W.

Matrix-heavy work speeds up: LLM prefill (+14–36% in
[#9](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/9),
[#15](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/15),
[#25](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/25) and
[#33](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/33)), diffusion and
FlashAttention. LLM decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth, and INT8
work stay about the same. The reports that compared outputs found them
bit-identical before and after.

Reports also cover up to four cards in one machine, the card driving the
display, and cards passed through to a VM with vfio-pci
([#17](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues/17)).




## How to install

First run:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock
cd gpu-unlock
make install
```

Then append `gpu_unlock.targets=all` to your kernel command line, keeping
existing options:

- **GRUB (Debian/Ubuntu/Mint):** add it inside `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT`
in `/etc/default/grub`, then run `sudo update-grub`.
- **GRUB (Arch/CachyOS):** same edit, then run
`sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg`.
- **Fedora/RHEL:** run
`sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="gpu_unlock.targets=all"`.
- **systemd-boot:** append it to the `options` line in your boot entry
(`bootctl status` shows its location).
- **UKI / generated entries:** add it to `/etc/kernel/cmdline` and regenerate
your boot images/entries (e.g. `sudo mkinitcpio -P` for mkinitcpio UKIs).



## Local build

Every build downloads the pinned NVIDIA/CachyOS inputs over HTTPS, checks
their SHA-256, and generates firmware only in the build directory and the
binary package. All three formats install through the same `make install-*`
targets. Packages are built from the committed `HEAD`.

Build, install build dependencies, and install the packages in one step
(asks for your sudo password):

```sh
make install        # detect the distribution and select an installer
make install-arch   # makepkg -sif
make install-deb    # apt-get build-dep, dpkg-buildpackage, apt-get install
make install-rpm    # dnf builddep, rpmbuild, dnf install
```

`make install` uses `/etc/os-release` (`ID`, then `ID_LIKE`) to detect Arch,
Debian/Ubuntu, or Fedora/RHEL/CentOS families. The RPM installer requires DNF.
For other distributions, select a compatible explicit target above.

`make arch`, `make deb` and `make rpm` only build. Debian and RPM packages go
to `build/deb` and `build/rpm`. The NVIDIA inputs are cached in
`~/.cache/gpu-unlock/inputs` (`make inputs`; override with `INPUTS=`).
`dpkg-buildpackage` itself never uses the network, so a clean-chroot build (sbuild or
pbuilder) needs `GPU_UNLOCK_INPUTS` pointing at that cache.
The `make dist` archive, the Debian source package and the `.nosrc.rpm`
contain no NVIDIA archives or generated firmware.

## Boot flow and opt-in

The packages put `gpu_unlock` and its firmware in the initramfs and load it
there, before `nvidia` can bind a card:

- **mkinitcpio:** `/etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/zz-gpu-unlock.conf` inserts
`gpu_unlock` right before `nvidia` in `MODULES`, so a display card is blank
for as short a time as possible. Without `nvidia` in the image, it goes
last and still runs before an `nvidia` loaded from the root filesystem.
Images are rebuilt on install. mkinitcpio ignores drop-ins for an image
built with `-c <config>` or a preset `_config`; put `gpu_unlock` right
before `nvidia` in that config's `MODULES` yourself.
- **initramfs-tools:** `/usr/share/initramfs-tools/modules.d/gpu-unlock.conf`.
- **dracut:** `/usr/lib/dracut/dracut.conf.d/gpu-unlock.conf`.

With initramfs-tools and dracut, the module is built for every installed
kernel that has headers, and those kernels' images are rebuilt on install
and again on removal. Kernels installed later get the module and a new
image from the kernel's own install hooks.

There is no `softdep nvidia pre:` rule: kmod honours only the first
`softdep nvidia` line it reads, so other packages' rules (`nvidia-utils`,
`gddr6_hwmon`) would silently override it, or it would override theirs.

The module does nothing unless the kernel command line opts in:

```
gpu_unlock.targets=all                          # every unbound GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 card
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0                 # only these cards
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0,0000:22:00.0    # comma-separated
```

Addresses are full PCI names as `lspci -D` prints them (hex digits in either
case), independent of GPU numbering and display role. An entry that is not
a GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 card, including `all` mixed with addresses, is logged and ignored.
The cards are unlocked concurrently, about a second in all however many
there are, and each on its own: a card that is already bound or powered
down is skipped. Bus mastering that the board firmware left on (Supermicro
X11 does this whatever its option ROM and bus master settings) is cleared
first; a card some driver already initialised is still refused. Then
`nvidia` loads and binds every card as usual.

The display card works too. Its firmware framebuffer (the boot console and
Plymouth) keeps running while the unlock's firmware steps run, and is
removed just before the card's reset, as `nvidia-drm` would do a moment
later anyway. Its screen is blank from that reset until `nvidia-drm` takes
over.

Loading the module by hand after boot does nothing to a card that `nvidia`
has bound.

Suspend to RAM powers the cards off, which resets the speed selectors. After
resume the module unlocks every card it unlocked at boot again, before
`nvidia` resumes it: its suspend notifier runs just ahead of the one `nvidia`
resumes its cards from (`NVreg_UseKernelSuspendNotifiers=1`, the default in
current drivers; `nvidia-resume.service` runs later still). This adds about a
second to resume. A card that kept power, as in suspend to idle, is still
unlocked and is only read. A card that `nvidia` has already resumed, or that is
bound to another driver, is left as it is, and the log says why. Add
`gpu_unlock.resume=0` to the kernel command line, or write `0` to
`/sys/module/gpu_unlock/parameters/resume`, to turn this off. Hibernation is
not covered.

Check the result with:

```sh
journalctl -k -b | grep gpu_unlock
lspci -nnk -s 0000:21:00.0
```

To stop unlocking, remove `gpu_unlock.targets=` from the kernel command line;
for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the
packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.

If the firmware on a card never stops, the module logs it and keeps the DMA
buffers that firmware may still use until the next power off. Power off
before trying again.

The kernel module and local packaging are GPL-2.0-only. The generated payload
derives from the pinned CMP reference; NVIDIA firmware remains under its own
terms. See `firmware/NOTICE.md` and `licenses/` for attribution and notices.

# MacNativeGames

Play your own Tears of the Kingdom and Breath of the Wild natively on Apple silicon Mac, iPhone and iPad.
Not an emulator: the game's own ARM64 code runs directly on Apple chips, and its NVN graphics are rebuilt on Metal.

# English **Breath of the Wild 1.6.0 and 1.9.0 are now officially supported on Mac!** 1.6.0 also runs on the iPhone (first played on an iPhone 14, October 23). **Tears of the Kingdom 1.0.0, 1.2.1 and 1.4.3 are now officially supported on Mac, iPhone and iPad!** > **Use your AI assistant to help you build the Mac app. We recommend Claude Code, Codex, or any other AI assistant you prefer.** [English](#english) | [中文](#chinese) ## Legal **You must own the game.** Use this project only with a copy of The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom that you bought, and with keys and system files dumped from your own Nintendo Switch. This is an independent, non-commercial project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Nintendo. The Legend of Zelda and Nintendo Switch are trademarks of Nintendo. The repository contains no game content and distributes none: no game program, art, text, audio, shaders or keys. Everything the game needs is made on your own computer from your own files when you build the app. The app you build contains the game, so it is for your own use only; do not share it. What the repository does hold is the information needed to make the port work: the patch code, the addresses and hashes used to check your files, and the [shared shader list](docs/shader-list.md), which names shaders and bind states but contains no shader code. Play your own copy of **The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom** natively on Apple silicon Mac, iPhone, and iPad. Bring your game file (XCI or NSP) and your `prod.keys`; one script builds a Mac app or an unsigned iPhone/iPad IPA. The iOS build requires iOS/iPadOS 26 and iPhone 14 or newer. It is not an emulator: the game's own ARM64 code runs directly on Apple chips (rewritten where the operating system requires it), the Switch system services are answered by a small host, and the game's NVN graphics are rebuilt on Metal. Nothing from the game is in this repository, and the project is not affiliated with Nintendo. Version 1.4.3 has been played on an iPhone 14 and an iPad; see [iPhone and iPad](docs/install.md#iphone-and-ipad). ## Let's maintain the shader list together: no more stutter > [!TIP] > **Every shader in the shared list is ready before you play.** On a Mac the game does not stop to compile it, and on an iPhone or iPad nothing is missing from the picture. The more places players cover, the smoother the game gets for everyone. The [shared shader list](docs/shader-list.md) now holds **34,937 shader variants** (28,464 shaders) from the Mac, iPhone and iPad: only states a build does not make by itself, since every build makes each shader's default variant. Every build makes them from the player's own game files, so the list holds identifiers only, never game data. Helping takes no setup: 1. **Play.** Every build carries each shader of the game for its default bind state. When your game meets a shader in a state that variant does not serve, or builds a render pipeline the app's list lacks, it notes it in `shader-list-contribution.txt`; default variants are never noted. 2. **On a Mac, every 100 new rows (shaders and pipelines together) it asks you once, before the game starts.** Click "Send": the GitHub form opens and the file is shown, ready to drag in. If the GitHub CLI (`gh`) is installed and signed in, the dialog offers "Submit automatically" instead, which sends this batch for you (a private gist and an issue) without opening the browser. An iPhone or iPad never asks during play: while it is connected to the Mac that built its app (cable or the same Wi-Fi), the Mac asks instead. "Don't remind me again" stops the reminders. 3. **Everyone's next build carries them.** Nobody stutters there again. **[Send your shaders →](https://github.com/ly05010419/MacNativeGames/issues/new?template=shader-list.yml)** · The game never uploads anything by itself. Update history: | Date | Platform | Update | |---|---|---| | Oct 23 | iPhone | **Breath of the Wild 1.6.0** on the iPhone: full screen, add-on content, saves copied from the Mac; both games render at 960x540 on the phone and use their own upscale to 1280x720 (no MetalFX) | | Oct 23 | Mac | **Super Mario Odyssey 1.3.0** (community port, early): Cap Kingdom and Bonneton playable at 60 fps on an M3, own runtime in [`games/odyssey`](games/odyssey/README.md), which has the build steps | | Oct 23 | iPhone, iPad | **Tears of the Kingdom** fills the screen, 60 fps by default, MetalFX upscaling | | Oct 23 | Mac | **Breath of the Wild 1.6.0**: key 2 interpolates again, and Link no longer shakes at 30+30; key 3 switches to native 2K; key 4 (21:9 ultrawide) and key 5 (edge smoothing) now work; every shader is prepared at build time, so far fewer translate in play | | Oct 23 | Mac | **Tears of the Kingdom** renders its 3D scene at the canvas resolution: internal 1920x1080 at 1080p (docked was only 1600x900), 2560x1440 on the 2K canvas | | Oct 21 | Mac | **Breath of the Wild 1.9.0**: shaders and render pipelines optimised | | Oct 21 | Mac, iPhone, iPad | **Tears of the Kingdom**: steadier at 90 fps, and steadier frame rates when no shaders are cached at all | | Oct 20 | Mac | **Breath of the Wild 1.9.0** (early): a base NSP and the 1.9.0 update NSP build the same app, each DLC pack optional (`--dlc`) | | Oct 20 | Mac | **Breath of the Wild 1.6.0** (early): a card image holding the base game, the update and the add-on content builds its own app with the same command; on a Mac, every 500 it asks to send them in a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/ly05010419/MacNativeGames/issues/new?template=shader-list.yml) | | Oct 19 | All | One shared [shader list](docs/shader-list.md); body:
# D2R Mobile **An open-source compatibility layer for Diablo II: Resurrected with the Reign of the Warlock expansion, for iOS, macOS, Android and HarmonyOS.** It brings the Nintendo Switch release you bought, expansion included, to iPhone, iPad and Mac in full: the original game code runs natively, every control is rebuilt for touch, the frame rate holds at 60 fps, and you are in a game one second after the main menu. There is now a native macOS version as well (first version): on an Apple silicon Mac it starts on double-click and works with keyboard, mouse and gamepad. **Since v2.0 there is an Android version** (community port): the same game program executes natively on ARM64 Android phones, with the graphics reimplemented on Vulkan; on a Snapdragon 8+ Gen 1 phone the camp and the Den of Evil and Cow Level fights all run at a median 60 fps (see "Android" below); a HarmonyOS version runs on the same engine (community port: an unsigned shell from the Releases page that you re-sign yourself, nothing to build; see "HarmonyOS"). Apple TV 4K (3rd generation, A15) has a community port (developer preview) that has reached the character-selection screen only on its author's device; see the device table below. This is not a tech demo that "sort of runs". It is a mobile version polished for daily play, from your first character all the way through the endgame. Platforms: iPhone / iPad (iOS 26 and later; iOS 18 – 25 with the older-API build) · Mac (Apple silicon, macOS 26 or later; macOS 15 – 25 with the older-API build) · Apple TV 4K (3rd generation, A15; community port, developer preview) · Android phones (ARM64, Android 12 or later, Vulkan 1.1; community port) · HarmonyOS phones (HarmonyOS NEXT; community port, unsigned shell from the Releases page that you re-sign yourself) · Game version: Switch release with Reign of the Warlock, 1.0.34.0 (corresponds to PC version 3.3.94012) · English / 中文 / Español / Русский / 한국어 · License: MIT · **Bring your own game files** 中文: [README.zh-CN.md](README.zh-CN.md) · Español: [README.es.md](README.es.md)

| 100% | 60 fps | about 1 s | about 3.8 W | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | The original gameplay, because it is the original program | Steady, with no drops once the device warms up | From the main menu into a game | Whole-device power draw at 60 fps | ## What it is, and what it is not **It is:** - The game's own aarch64 program, **executing directly on the device**, with no emulated CPU. iPhone and Switch use the same class of processor; only the handful of instructions that cannot run unchanged under Apple's kernel are rewritten, and every other byte of the program is left exactly as shipped. Every class, every Runeword, Terror Zones, bosses, drop rules and quest flow are identical to the original. - The platform services the game expects — system calls, the file system, the graphics API, audio, input — provided by a small host written for Apple platforms. The graphics API is reimplemented entirely — on Metal on Apple devices, on Vulkan on Android — with no emulation layer in between, and the shaders are translated offline from the game's originals. - A port built for phones, and taken all the way: a complete touch control scheme, edge-to-edge iPhone and true full-screen iPad display, controller support, a power saver mode, save sync, five languages (English, Chinese, Spanish, Russian and Korean), and a whole set of endgame modes and quality-of-life features the original never had. **It is not:** - An emulator, cloud gaming, or streaming. - **A source of game content. It contains none and distributes none.** There is no game program, art, text, data table or shader in this repository; all of that is generated on your own machine from your own files (see [docs/GAME_FILES.md](docs/GAME_FILES.md)). What the repository does carry is the interface information we recorded to make the port work — shader interface descriptions, the graphics API function table, addresses inside the program and the like — listed item by item in [docs/DERIVED.md](docs/DERIVED.md). - Online. There is no multiplayer; the game runs fully offline and needs no online account. ## Battle-tested All **44** iPhones and iPads in the closed beta — 35 devices registered for direct install (25 iPhones and 10 iPads), plus 9 TestFlight accounts with one device each — **completed Normal, Nightmare and Hell with multiple characters**, and the experience was excellent. From an iPhone 14 Pro Max with 6 GB of memory to the latest iPad Pro, not one device fell behind. | | Models | |---|---| | iPhone | 14 Pro Max, 15, 15 Pro, 15 Pro Max, 16 Plus, 16 Pro, 16 Pro Max, 17 Pro Max and more | | iPad | iPad Air, iPad mini, iPad Pro 11-inch and 12.9 / 13-inch (including M2 and M4) and more | | Lowest model tested | **iPhone 14 Pro Max (A16, 6 GB): a flawless 60 fps** | iPhone and iPad share a single install package.

## Fast, smooth, and easy on the battery Measured on a real device (iPhone 17 Pro Max): | Item | Reading | |---|---| | In-game frame rate | **60 fps**, steady, with no drops once the device warms up | | App launch | 0.15 s | | To the main menu | about 1 s | | From the main menu into a game | **about 1 s** | | Quick Restart, back in a game | about 1.2 s | | Longest frame when changing acts | about 0.1 s | | Whole-device power, 60 fps | **about 3.8 W** (in camp, 50% brightness): nearly 5 hours of continuous play on a full charge | | Whole-device power, power saver mode at 30 fps | **about 1.85 W**, about half the 60 fps figure, for about twice the battery life | Measurement conditions: power is whole-device power measured on 2026-10-10 on an iPhone 17 Pro Max, standing in the Act I camp at 50% brightness, with 60 fps and power saver mode measured in the same scene; battery life is calculated from the measured power and the battery capacity, not by playing from full to empty. Launch and game-entry times were measured on the same model in 2026-10; frame rate and act-change readings were taken on the same model on 2026-10-12 while moving through areas and changing acts after entering a game. The install package is only a little over 100 MB. The game resources (about 5.6 GB) are placed on the phone separately, and updating the app touches neither your saves nor the resources. Why it is this fast: the program executes natively, and not a single instruction goes through emulation; graphics go straight to Metal; every shader is translated offline and compiled ahead of time, so nothing is compiled when you enter a new scene. Older chips (A16 and earlier, such as the iPhone 14 family and iPhone 15) do not support the game's original compressed texture format; they need an extra texture pack made from your own game files, and then run at full frame rate too — see [docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md](docs/LEGACY_DEVICES.md). ## Redesigned for fingers This is not a gamepad pasted onto the screen. Every panel and every action was rebuilt for fingers under one design principle: **keep the original interface language, and use gestures instead of adding buttons to the screen**. Text sizes and tap targets are sized for fingers. You know how to play the moment you pick it up, and it stays comfortable over long sessions.

- **Move**: a virtual stick with precise diagonals; tap an NPC or the ground to path there automatically; doors, portals and cave entrances are tappable across their whole surface. - **Fight**: press a skill button to cast, hold to keep casting, **drag to aim at any angle**; nearby monsters are targeted automatically. Two skill sets. Skills on your secondary weapons cast with one tap — the game swaps weapons, casts, and swaps back — and the button shows the charges remaining. - **Boss health bar**: pinned to the top of the screen, showing the percentage remaining. - **Items**: tap, double-tap, long-press and drag and drop all track your finger. Double-tap gear to equip or unequip it; drag an item anywhere onto the vendor panel to sell it; on a stack, double-tap takes 1 and long-press takes 3; long-press an empty inventory slot to sort everything. - **Text**: typed with the system keyboard. Character names can be in Chinese; leave the name blank for a random one. - **Screen**: on iPhone the 19.5:9 display is filled edge to edge, clear of the notch and rounded corners; on iPad the game fills the entire screen, and the interface centers itself when you open a panel; the 3D picture can be brightened. ### Controller Connect a controller and press any button: the interface switches to the original controller layout, with button prompts at the bottom of every panel. Touch the screen and you are back in the touch interface instantly. Inventory, stash, skill tree, Chronicle and settings are fully controller-navigable, with the same button mapping as on Switch. With an Xbox controller the layout switches automatically to the PC / Xbox one (bottom confirms, right goes back) and the prompts show Xbox button icons; there is nothing to turn on. With a PlayStation controller (DualSense or DualShock 4) the prompts switch to the game's own PlayStation button icons (✕ confirms, ○ goes back), contributed by [@Ti800](https://github.com/Ti800) ([#119](https://github.com/jhaizhou-ops/d2r-mobile/pull/119)).

## New ways to play, on top of the original Finishing the original game is only the beginning. Without touching the original rules, we added a full set of endgame content that keeps you farming. ### Greater Rift Enter through the red portal in Harrogath after completing Hell. There are 100 levels, and the monsters grow stronger with each one; fill the progress bar and slay the Rift Guardian within 15 minutes to clear a level. Every 2 levels cleared grants +1 Skill Point and +5 Stat Points, and the skill level cap rises from 20 to 40. Every 10 levels has a first-clear reward, and clearing level 10 unlocks six new equipment slots for your mercenary.

### Endgame Boss Rush, Elysium mode, and the Kill Board - **Endgame Boss Rush**: unlocks after completing Hell, with 12 stages; stage 11 is Diablo Clone, and stage 12 is the three Uber bosses. - **Elysium mode** (chosen at character creation): Unique ×5, Set ×3, Runes ×5; the "no drop" chance is cut to a tenth, and bosses always drop as on a first kill. - **Kill Board**: for every boss, the number of kills, the time of the first kill, how many Unique and Set items it has dropped, and your best and average kill times.

### Storage: a collector's paradise - **Chronicle stash**: every identified Unique and Set item has its own fixed slot, shared by all characters, searchable, with deposit and withdraw; the Deposit button sends the Unique and Set items in your inventory and Horadric Cube there in one tap. - **Stash**: widened to 14 columns, with 5 personal pages and 5 shared pages. - **Trove**: the gem, rune and material pages merged into one, with the Horadric Cube's crafting grid in the middle, so finding things and crafting no longer means flipping between pages. Runes, gems and materials you put into the personal or shared pages are filed here automatically. - **Pouch**: an extended inventory. Runes and gems found in the field go into it automatically and take up no inventory space.

### Effortless farming | | | |---|---| | Auto-recast buffs | Buff skills you have learned do not need a slot on the skill bar: when a buff runs out, it is recast the moment you stand still; buffs that come from your secondary weapons (such as Battle Orders from Call to Arms) swap weapons, recast and swap back on their own | | Potions and belt | Auto-drink has two tiers: a healing potion below 50% Life, a rejuvenation potion below 30%; **your mercenary is fed automatically by the same rule**. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR G["Your game files
(program + resources)"] --> P["Rewriter
changes only a few instructions"] G --> S["Shader translation
original → Metal"] P --> H["Host
system services"] S --> X["Graphics layer
the graphics API on Metal"] H --> A["iOS app
touch and interface"] X --> A ``` | Part | Where | What it does | |---|---|---| | Program rewriter | `dm/tools/patch_nso.py` | Rewrites only the few instructions that cannot run unchanged under Apple's kernel (thread-pointer registers, system calls, timers) and leaves the rest of the program byte-for-byte as shipped | | Host | `dm/host` | Loads the rewritten program and provides the platform services it calls | | Graphics | `dm/gfx` | Implements the game's graphics API on Metal; shaders are translated offline from the game's originals | | iOS app | `dm/ios` | The app shell, touch controls and interface | | Android app | `dm/android` | The Android shell, touch overlay and Vulkan presentation | | HarmonyOS app | `dm/harmony` | The HarmonyOS shell (ArkTS + N-API), sharing the host and the Vulkan engine with Android | | Vulkan graphics | `dm/gfx/vulkan` | The same graphics API on Vulkan (shared by Android and HarmonyOS; the engine comes from the HarmonyOS port) | | Verification | `dm/verify` | Checks that the rewritten code behaves exactly like the original, plus the regression gates every change goes through | **Why you can trust it:** the stability is not luck. The test and verification tooling is part of the project — unit tests for the host and graphics layers, an equivalence check for every rewritten instruction, scripted walkthrough regression for the touch interface, and on-device smoke tests. Start with `make -C dm/host/tests run`, `make -C dm/gfx/tests run` and `dm/verify/regress.sh` (run them inside the Python environment prepared in step 2 below; `regress.sh` also needs `brew install llvm`). How to contribute is in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Android (new in v2.0) Android phones use ARM64 processors just like the Switch, so, as on Apple devices, the game's own program executes directly on the phone with no CPU emulation. The host has some behaviour that is on by default on iOS and was written for this one game; another game runs into these first, so turn them off or move them out before you start: - `dm/host/hle_oe.c`: the 3D render scale defaults to 0.75 on phones (the Android app sets 0.85), and `scale3d_tick` rewrites it at offsets inside this game's renderer — with another game that is a wild pointer. - `dm/host/hle_fs.c`: seeding the shared stash on first launch (`DM_STASH_SEED`) and the touch-layout default settings (`DM_TOUCH_DEFAULTS`) are on by default on iOS. - `dm/host/main.c`: the save-flush throttle patches a constant at a fixed address in the game program; `argv[0]` is hard-coded to `"D2R"`. - `dm/host/hle_time.c`: the fixed-time test switch recognises a fixed address in the game program. - `front_game_res` in `dm/host/front_mac.m`: the docked / handheld resolutions are hard-coded to 1600×900 / 1280×720. - `dm/host/dm_cloudsync.c`: character directories are recognised by `.d2s`. - `dm/host/dm_cursor.c` and `dm/host/dm_world.c`: the whole files are specific to this game. additions welcome) | | [docs/DERIVED.md](docs/DERIVED.md) | Game-related material in this repository: what is here, what is not, and why | | [docs/ANDROID.md](docs/ANDROID.md) | Playing on an Android phone: installing the APK, making the import pack, new releases, troubleshooting | | [docs/HARMONYOS.md](docs/HARMONYOS.md) | Playing on a HarmonyOS phone: re-signing the unsigned shell, making the runtime pack, importing, troubleshooting | | [dm/harmony/README.md](dm/harmony/README.md) | HarmonyOS: source layout, build commands, defaults and measurements | | [dm/android/README.md](dm/android/README.md) | Android: source layout, building, the files to put on the phone, the acceptance checklist | | [dm/gfx/vulkan/INTEGRATION.md](dm/gfx/vulkan/INTEGRATION.md) | How the Vulkan graphics layer plugs into the shared graphics API | | [docs/ANDROID_COLLABORATION.md](docs/ANDROID_COLLABORATION.md) | Android / HarmonyOS collaboration: who works where, how to take part, measured status and remaining work; the notes from every round are in [docs/android-notes/](docs/android-notes/) | ## Legal **You must own the game, including the Reign of the Warlock expansion.** This is an independent, non-commercial project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Blizzard Entertainment or Nintendo. Diablo and Blizzard Entertainment are trademarks of Blizzard Entertainment, Inc.; Nintendo Switch is a trademark of Nintendo. Use it only with a copy of the game that you own. ## Acknowledgements **The Android version in v2.0 comes from three community authors. Special thanks to:** - **[@yyan160](https://github.com/yyan160)** (Yuechuan Yang): the Android port itself ([#113](https://github.com/jhaizhou-ops/d2r-mobile/pull/113)) — the Android app, the JNI host, the touch overlay, Vulkan presentation, a full round of performance work measured step by step on a phone (the Redmi K50 Ultra camp went from 7.7 fps to a median 60 fps), and the changes that let the shared host build and run on both Apple and Android. Every point raised in review was fixed on the branch. - **[@biglawine](https://github.com/biglawine)**: the HarmonyOS port ([#114](https://github.com/jhaizhou-ops/d2r-mobile/pull/114)) and its NVN-to-Vulkan replay engine, which is where the Android graphics layer comes from; they also set up the Android / HarmonyOS collaboration repositories and generated the shader bundles used for on-device testing. - **[@vickwv](https://github.com/vickwv)**: a separate, independent Android port ([#112](https://github.com/jhaizhou-ops/d2r-mobile/pull/112)). Its ideas were each measured on the Android version, and its 3D brightening approach was adopted. This project stands on the open-source work below. Thank you to its authors and maintainers. - **Ryujinx** (Ryubing 1.3.2, MIT): `dm/third_party/ryujinx` bundles its shader translator unchanged (the Ryujinx.Graphics.Shader, Spv.Generator and Ryujinx.Common projects), which translates the Switch game's shaders to SPIR-V. During development we also ran the original game in a patched Ryujinx as the reference for comparing pictures and game state (see [dm/verify/README.md](dm/verify/README.md); the scripts that build and drive it are not in this repository). - **deko3d** (devkitPro, zlib): the texture layout size algorithm in `dm/gfx/nvn/nvn_tex.c` is ported from it. - **nvn.h** (h1k421, MIT): the graphics API declarations in `dm/gfx/nvn/include/nvn.h`. - **libdeflate** (Eric Biggers, MIT): decompressing game data. - **bcdec** (iOrange, MIT or Unlicense): decoding BC textures on devices that do not support the BC formats. - **FLIP** (NVIDIA, BSD 3-Clause): the image difference metric used in image-quality checks. - **Offline fix patch** (LFS Mod Offline Fix): the 7 rewrites in `dm/tools/patch_nso.py` that let the game run offline come from this community patch. We have no reliable record of where it was first published or who wrote it; if you know, please open an Issue. - Tools used to build and verify: SPIRV-Cross (SPIR-V to Metal Shading Language), XcodeGen, .NET, Capstone and Unicorn (disassembly and equivalence checks of the rewrites), Pillow, numpy, lz4, astcenc (the Legacy Device Pack), hactool (extracting files from a game package), libimobiledevice and LLVM.
